name: United States
governanceModel: Sectoral and executive-led, with significant state-level activity
debateTopics: Who leads AI policy after the AI czar role went vacant
Federal preemption vs. state AI laws
overview:
The United States regulates AI mainly through existing sectoral agencies and executive action rather than a single federal law. Since January 2025, federal policy has moved in a broadly deregulatory direction: the prior administration's safety-testing executive order was repealed, and the current administration's America's AI Action Plan (released July 2025) emphasises infrastructure build-out and export of the US AI stack over precautionary rules.

In the absence of comprehensive federal legislation, states remain a major source of binding AI rules, though even flagship state laws are in flux — Colorado's original AI Act was repealed and replaced with a narrower version in May 2026 before it ever took effect. At the federal level, NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) has been one of the most active federal AI bodies, expanding its voluntary model-testing relationships with frontier labs through 2026.

atAGlance.governmentInvolvement: Low-to-moderate — light federal touch, no binding frontier-model law

currentDirection.summary: Federal AI policy leadership arguably thinned rather than tightened through 2026 — the White House AI & Crypto Czar role has sat vacant since David Sacks stepped down in March, leaving CAISI's technical standards and testing work as one of the most active and consistent threads of federal AI policy activity.

recentDevelopments.text: FTC opens public comment on an AI-accuracy and manipulation policy statement, issued pursuant to Executive Order 14365; a bipartisan 'Great American AI Act' (GAAIA) discussion draft circulates in Congress; the House Science Committee advances ten AI bills, including one that would statutorily codify CAISI.
CAISI signs pre-deployment testing agreements with Google DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI, extending arrangements it already held with OpenAI and Anthropic.

CAISI publishes a technical evaluation of DeepSeek's V4 Pro model, finding it lags top US frontier models by roughly eight months in aggregate capability while remaining the most capable PRC model evaluated to date.

Colorado Governor Jared Polis signs SB 26-189, repealing and replacing the Colorado AI Act (SB 24-205) with a narrower disclosure/transparency framework for automated decision-making; the duty of care, mandatory risk-management programs, impact-assessment requirements and AG-reporting obligations of the original law are dropped, and the new effective date is pushed to January 1, 2027.

David Sacks steps down as White House AI & Crypto Czar after reaching the 130-day limit for special government employees; moves to co-chair the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology instead. No successor had been named as of mid-2026.
CAISI signs an MOU with the General Services Administration on federal AI procurement standards.
Anthropic launches the Anthropic Institute; Jack Clark moves from Head of Policy to Head of Public Benefit to lead it, while Sarah Heck becomes Head of Public Policy.
CAISI launches an AI Agent Standards Initiative to develop evaluation benchmarks for autonomous AI agents.
House Science Committee advances ten AI-related bills, including one that would statutorily codify CAISI (currently operating on voluntary MOUs rather than statutory authority).

policyAndRegulation.title: Colorado AI Act (SB 24-205 → SB 26-189)
policyAndRegulation.summary: Colorado's original SB 24-205 established a duty of care, mandatory risk-management programs, and impact-assessment requirements for high-risk AI used in consequential decisions (employment, credit, housing, healthcare). That law was repealed and replaced by SB 26-189, signed by Governor Jared Polis on May 14, 2026, which drops the duty of care, risk-management-program, impact-assessment and attorney-general-reporting requirements in favour of a narrower disclosure/transparency framework for automated decision-making. SB 26-189 takes effect January 1, 2027.

policyAndRegulation.title: California AB 2013 — Training Data Transparency
policyAndRegulation.summary: Requires developers of generative AI systems made available to Californians to publicly disclose a high-level summary of the datasets used to train the system; took effect January 1, 2026. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have published disclosures. xAI (now SpaceXAI) sued California Attorney General Rob Bonta in December 2025 challenging the law's constitutionality; a district court denied a preliminary-injunction motion in March 2026, and the case remained under Ninth Circuit review as of mid-2026.

policyAndRegulation.title: TAKE IT DOWN Act
policyAndRegulation.summary: Federal law criminalising the publication of non-consensual intimate imagery, including AI-generated deepfakes, and requiring platforms to remove reported content within 48 hours of a valid notice. Signed into law May 19, 2025; the notice-and-removal requirement took effect one year later, on May 19, 2026, with FTC enforcement authority.

policyAndRegulation.title: Great American AI Act (GAAIA) — discussion draft
policyAndRegulation.summary: A bipartisan 269-page discussion draft released June 4, 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), proposing frontier-model disclosure and third-party-audit requirements alongside a three-year federal preemption of state laws that regulate AI model 'development' (though not deployment); not yet introduced as a formal bill.

researchEcosystem.summary: US AI research remains among the world's largest and most influential, anchored by Stanford HAI, MIT CSAIL, and a dense private-lab research ecosystem; many observers argue private labs increasingly outpace university output at the frontier. Federal programmes like the National AI Research Resource pilot aim to broaden compute access for academic researchers who can't match private labs' training-scale infrastructure.

companies.description: Developer of the Grok model family. SpaceX acquired xAI in an all-stock deal announced February 2026, and by July 2026 the entity had formally rebranded as SpaceXAI, a SpaceX subsidiary. It signed its CAISI pre-deployment testing agreement in May 2026 under the xAI name.

debates.topic: Who leads AI policy after the AI czar role went vacant
debates.summary: David Sacks's move from White House AI & Crypto Czar to a PCAST co-chair role in March 2026 left the position without a direct successor, raising questions about who actually coordinates federal AI policy.
debates.expanded: Sacks reached the 130-day cap on his special-government-employee status and shifted to advising through PCAST rather than the White House directly. No replacement AI czar had been named as of mid-2026. In practice, OSTP Director Michael Kratsios and CAISI appear to have absorbed part of the coordinating role, but the absence of a dedicated czar has drawn commentary about whether AI policy now lacks a single accountable owner inside the administration.

debates.topic: Federal preemption vs. state AI laws
debates.summary: Industry and parts of the federal government are pushing for a single national standard to override the growing patchwork of state AI laws; states have so far resisted ceding their own rules, even as some flagship state laws are themselves being narrowed or challenged in court.
debates.expanded: Colorado and California have moved fastest on binding state AI rules, though Colorado's original SB 24-205 duty-of-care framework was repealed and replaced by the narrower SB 26-189 in May 2026 (effective January 1, 2027) before it ever took effect. California's AB 2013 training-data disclosure law is being challenged by xAI (now SpaceXAI), which sued Attorney General Rob Bonta in December 2025 arguing the law is unconstitutional; a district court denied a preliminary injunction in March 2026, and the case remains under Ninth Circuit review. Industry groups argue a fragmented state-by-state patchwork raises compliance costs and slows deployment, and have lobbied for federal preemption; the bipartisan GAAIA discussion draft proposes a three-year federal preemption of state laws that regulate AI model development (though not deployment), and in July 2026 the FTC's proposed AI-accuracy policy statement — issued under Executive Order 14365 — specifically flagged Colorado's AI Act as a law that could be preempted. States'-rights advocates and consumer groups counter that preemption without a substantive federal replacement would leave a regulatory vacuum.

debates.summary: Multiple lawsuits against OpenAI, Meta, and Stability AI over training on copyrighted material are testing the boundaries of fair use.
debates.expanded: Authors, news publishers, and visual artists have brought a wave of suits arguing that training foundation models on their copyrighted work without licence is infringement; AI developers argue it falls under fair use as transformative. Early rulings have been mixed, and the issue is expected to reach appellate courts before a clear precedent is set.

debates.summary: Ongoing dispute over how tightly to restrict advanced AI chip exports, particularly to China, without ceding global AI infrastructure market share.
debates.expanded: Successive rounds of export controls have restricted sales of NVIDIA's and AMD's most advanced chips to China, aiming to slow rival AI capability growth. Critics argue restrictions push Chinese buyers toward domestic alternatives (accelerating China's own chip industry) and cede market share; national security officials argue the controls meaningfully slow adversary progress.

debates.summary: CAISI has become one of the most substantive checks on frontier AI models in the US, now holding pre-deployment testing agreements with five major labs.
debates.expanded: With OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI (which announced its agreement under that name before its July 2026 rebrand to SpaceXAI) all now under some form of CAISI pre-deployment testing arrangement, the agency is often described as the closest thing the US currently has to a binding frontier-model check — even though the arrangements are voluntary agreements rather than statutory requirements, and could in principle be unwound without legislative action.
